seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #5 — Never Install Python By Hand Again (2026)
altTitles: uv python install, pin and list explained
seo.description: Chapter five of the uv course. Managed versus system interpreters, uv python install and list, python-build-standalone, .python-version and how it is searched upwards, and why uv picks the first compatible version rather than the newest.
seo.breakdown: how uv downloads and manages Python versions for you, pins one per project, and never touches the interpreters it merely found.

scenes.narration: How many Pythons are on your laptop right now? Most people guess wrong.

I asked this machine, and the answer was three. One from an installer years ago, one from a science distribution, and one that came with the operating system. None of them knew about the others. That's a completely normal laptop, by the way.

uvStage.headline: Three, on a [normal] laptop
uvStage.premise: Three interpreters from three sources, none of which knows about the others.

steps.label: uv python list --only-installed
steps.detail: three, and nobody planned any of them

stage.label: cpython-3.9.9
stage.sub: also from python.org, also years ago

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter hands the whole problem of installing Python over to uv, so you never download an installer from a website again.

data.title: Let uv own your Pythons
data.subtitle: uv, chapter five · the rack, and the pin

scenes.narration: First, the distinction that makes everything else make sense.

Interpreters get sorted into two piles, and the split matters because it decides what uv is allowed to change. A system Python was already on the machine when uv arrived, so uv will happily use one but will never modify it. A managed Python is one uv downloaded itself, into uv's own folder, which means uv can add and remove those freely.

uvStage.headline: Two piles: [managed] and system
uvStage.premise: uv uses what it finds and owns only what it fetched. The line never moves.

steps.label: uv python dir
steps.detail: everything uv owns lives in here

stage.label: cpython-3.13.1
stage.sub: downloaded by uv, into uv folder

scenes.narration: And the headline behaviour, straight from the documentation: uv will automatically download Python versions when they are required. You've already watched that happen in chapter four. No installer, no website, no wizard — the version you asked for simply turns up.

uvStage.headline: It fetches them [automatically]
uvStage.premise: Ask for a version. If uv does not have it, uv gets it and carries on.

steps.label: uv python install 3.12
steps.detail: four seconds, and no browser involved

stage.label: cpython-3.12.14
stage.sub: four seconds ago it was not here

scenes.narration: You can name several versions at once, and you can name implementations other than the usual one. PyPy and GraalPy are alternative Pythons with different performance characteristics, which means the same code can behave quite differently on each — and uv fetches either with exactly the same command.

uvStage.headline: Several, and [other] Pythons
uvStage.premise: One command, many versions — and CPython is not the only implementation.

steps.label: uv python install 3.11 3.12 3.13
steps.detail: three interpreters, one command

steps.label: uv python install pypy@3.11
steps.detail: a different implementation entirely

steps.label: uv python list --only-installed | wc -l
steps.detail: six interpreters, none of them by hand

scenes.narration: Now the command you'll actually type most often.

Running uv python list prints the whole rack. Every line is a version, and the right-hand column is the interesting bit: either a real path, meaning that interpreter is already here, or the words download available, meaning uv can have it in a few seconds if you ask.

uvStage.headline: Read the [right-hand] column
uvStage.premise: A path means it is here. "download available" means uv can fetch it.

steps.label: uv python list
steps.detail: a path, or an offer

stage.label: cpython-3.15.0rc1
stage.sub: not out yet, and already reachable

stage.label: cpython-3.10.4
stage.sub: a real path, already on the machine

scenes.narration: One detail is worth knowing before you rely on any of this. The interpreters don't come from python dot org. Instead, uv uses a project called python-build-standalone, which produces portable builds designed to run from any folder at all. That portability is exactly why uv can drop an interpreter into its own directory and have it work immediately.

uvStage.headline: Not from [python.org]
uvStage.premise: Portable builds, designed to run from any folder rather than one fixed place.

steps.label: ls "$(uv python dir)"
steps.detail: one folder per interpreter, movable

stage.label: your package manager
stage.sub: ties the version to your OS release

stage.label: python-build-standalone
stage.sub: runs from wherever you put it

stage.label: uv python dir
stage.sub: which is why uv can just drop one in

scenes.narration: And here is the part that makes a project reproducible rather than merely lucky.

Running uv python pin writes a tiny file called dot python dash version into the folder you're standing in. From then on, every uv command run in that project uses the version named in that file. Commit the file, and your colleague gets the same interpreter without being told.

uvStage.headline: One tiny file [decides] it
uvStage.premise: .python-version names the interpreter, and every uv command in the folder obeys.

steps.label: uv python pin 3.12
steps.detail: one line of text, in one small file

steps.label: cat .python-version && uv run python -V
steps.detail: and every command here now obeys it

scenes.narration: That file gets searched for in the folder you're standing in and in every parent above it. Which means a pin at the top of a repository covers every project inside, and a pin inside one project overrides the one above. Nearest wins, which is the rule you'd expect anyway.

uvStage.headline: Nearest [pin] wins
uvStage.premise: uv looks in this folder, then every parent. The closest file is the one obeyed.

steps.label: cd invoice-app && uv run python -V
steps.detail: the nearer pin won

stage.label: .python-version
stage.sub: and this one overrides the parent

scenes.narration: Two behaviours here surprise people, so let's say both plainly. First: uv uses the first compatible version, not the newest one. If your project needs three point ten or better, and three point ten is sitting there, uv takes three point ten and does not go looking for anything shinier.

uvStage.headline: First compatible, not [newest]
uvStage.premise: uv takes the earliest version that satisfies you, not the highest one available.

steps.label: uv run python -V
steps.detail: not 3.13, even though 3.13 is right there

scenes.narration: Second: installing a Python with uv doesn't put a bare python command on your PATH. That's deliberate, because silently replacing the python command on somebody's machine is exactly the kind of surprise uv refuses to spring. If you genuinely want that, dash dash default asks for it explicitly.

uvStage.headline: No bare [python] on your PATH
uvStage.premise: uv will not shadow a command you already depend on unless you ask it to.

steps.label: uv python install 3.13 && which python3
steps.detail: still your original python3

steps.label: uv python install 3.13 --default --preview
steps.detail: now, and only now, uv adds them

stage.label: uv run python
stage.sub: the safe way to reach uv Python

stage.label: --default
stage.sub: only when you say so, out loud

scenes.narration: There's a related file worth not confusing with the pin. The pin says which Python to use. Requires-python, over in pyproject dot toml, says which Pythons your code is allowed to run on at all — a promise to everybody else, rather than a choice for you.

uvStage.headline: The pin, and the [promise]
uvStage.premise: One file chooses for you. The other declares what your code supports for everyone.
uvStage.token: they are not the same field

steps.label: grep requires-python pyproject.toml
steps.detail: a promise about what your code supports

steps.label: cat .python-version
steps.detail: and a choice about what you develop on

scenes.narration: Every command that runs Python takes the same flag, which is genuinely useful when you're checking whether a bug is version-specific. Add dash dash python and a number to uv run, and the whole thing runs on that interpreter instead — without changing anything you've pinned.

uvStage.headline: Try it on [another] version
uvStage.premise: One flag reruns the same code on a different interpreter, changing nothing.

steps.label: uv run main.py
steps.detail: on the pinned 3.12, as usual

steps.label: uv run --python 3.9 main.py
steps.detail: and now you know it is version-specific

stage.label: cpython-3.9.9
stage.sub: which is the answer you wanted

scenes.narration: And once uv owns your interpreters, that chapter-zero mess starts to clear on its own. Every project names the version it wants, uv fetches whatever is missing, and nobody ever downloads an installer from a website and forgets which folder it went into.

uvStage.headline: The mess, [cleared] up
uvStage.premise: Each project names its version. uv fetches what is missing. Nothing is guessed.

steps.label: cat */.python-version
steps.detail: each project states its own answer

scenes.narration: Quick check. Your project needs three point ten or newer, and both three point ten and three point thirteen are installed. Which does uv pick? Pause the video here and commit to an answer before I say it. Ready? Three point ten — first compatible, never newest.

quiz.question: requires-python >=3.10, and 3.10 and 3.13 installed. Which runs?
quiz.why: The first compatible one. Pin a version if you want a specific one.

scenes.narration: Managed Pythons come and go like anything else uv owns. Uninstall removes one, list shows what's left, and none of it ever reaches the interpreters your operating system depends on. Which means you can try a release candidate on a Tuesday and be rid of it by Wednesday.

uvStage.headline: Fetched, used, [removed]
uvStage.premise: uv only ever removes what uv fetched. Your system interpreters are off limits.

steps.label: uv python install 3.15.0rc1
steps.detail: a release candidate, on a Tuesday

steps.label: uv python uninstall 3.15.0rc1
steps.detail: and gone again, by Wednesday

steps.label: which python3
steps.detail: your system Python never noticed

scenes.narration: So, to recap. uv separates interpreters it merely found from interpreters it downloaded, and only ever changes the second kind. A one-line file pins a project to a version and travels with the repository. And uv takes the first compatible version, not the newest one.

points.text: Found ones are used. Fetched ones are owned.
First compatible version, never the newest
